questions.stem: How many carbon atoms does the stem pent stand for?

options.explanation: Pent is the fifth stem: meth 1, eth 2, prop 3, but 4, pent 5.
Four carbons is the stem but, one step below pent.
Six carbons is hex, the stem above pent.
Three carbons is prop, which shares no letters with pent worth trusting.

questions.stem: What information does the suffix of an organic name carry?

options.text: Which functional group the compound carries
options.explanation: The end part of the name names the reactive group, such as ene for a C=C bond.

options.text: How many carbon atoms are in the chain
options.explanation: Carbon counting belongs to the stem at the front of the name.

options.text: The boiling point of the compound
options.explanation: Physical data never appears in the name; the suffix is structural information.

options.text: The state of the compound at room temperature
options.explanation: State is a physical property; the suffix records the functional group instead.

questions.stem: Which name matches a 2-carbon molecule with a C=C double bond?

options.text: Ethene
options.explanation: Eth gives two carbons and ene gives the double bond, so the assembly is ethene.

options.text: Methene
options.explanation: One carbon cannot carry a C=C bond, and meth is the wrong stem for two carbons.

options.text: Ethane
options.explanation: The suffix ane means no special group; the double bond demands ene.

options.text: Ethanediol
options.explanation: That name points to an alcohol-family compound, not a 2-carbon alkene.

questions.stem: A molecule named butanol contains how many carbon atoms, and which family?

options.text: 4 carbon atoms, the alcohol family
options.explanation: The stem but counts four carbons and the suffix anol places it in the alcohol family.

options.text: 4 carbon atoms, the alkene family
options.explanation: Alkenes carry the suffix ene; anol signals the alcohol group instead.

options.text: 3 carbon atoms, the alcohol family
options.explanation: Three carbons would be propanol; but always means four.

options.text: 5 carbon atoms, the alkane family
options.explanation: Five carbons is pent, and alkanes end in ane, neither of which matches butanol.

questions.stem: Why do IUPAC rules matter for naming compounds?

options.text: They give every compound one unambiguous name scientists worldwide can use
options.explanation: A shared rulebook means a name reconstructs the same structure in any laboratory.

options.text: They shorten all names to three letters
options.explanation: The rules aim for precision, not brevity; names grow longer as structures grow richer.

options.text: They let chemists rename compounds daily
options.explanation: The opposite is true: fixed rules keep names stable over time.

options.text: They only apply to compounds with six or more carbons
options.explanation: The rules apply throughout; six carbons is just the exam expectation ceiling.

questions.stem: Give the number of carbon atoms signalled by the stem hex.
Name the suffix that signals an O-H group on the chain.
questions.modelAnswer: The suffix -anol marks the alcohol family, as in methanol.

questions.stem: Explain how the name methanol tells you both the chain length and the family of the molecule.
questions.modelAnswer: The stem meth counts one carbon atom and the suffix -anol shows the alcohol group, so the single name encodes both facts at once.

questions.stem: An unknown straight-chain molecule has six carbons and one C=C bond. Write its name.
questions.modelAnswer: Hexene - hex for the six carbons, -ene for the double bond.

questions.stem: Why are the carbon atoms in a chain numbered when naming?

options.text: To record exactly which carbon carries the functional group
options.explanation: The number in the name is the address of the reactive group on the chain.

options.text: To count the total number of atoms in the molecule
options.explanation: Total counting is the stem job; numbering is about position along the chain.

options.text: To show the order in which the atoms were discovered
options.explanation: Discovery order never enters the naming system.

options.text: To rank the atoms by reactivity
options.explanation: Numbering locates groups; it does not rank them.

questions.stem: A molecule carries two identical functional groups. How is its name adjusted?

options.text: The prefix di- is added to the second part of the name
options.explanation: Two identical groups are flagged with di- before the suffix part of the name.

options.text: The suffix is deleted because groups cancel out
options.explanation: Groups never cancel; both must be reflected in the name.

options.text: The stem is doubled instead of the suffix
options.explanation: The doubling convention attaches to the second part of the name, not the stem.

options.text: The name is left unchanged because groups share one position
options.explanation: Two groups need two positions recorded; silence would misdescribe the molecule.

questions.stem: How does the naming system cope with isomers?

options.text: The same rules applied to each structure produce different, correct names
options.explanation: Because the rules encode chain length and group position, each arrangement earns its own name.

options.text: Isomers all share one name because their formula matches
options.explanation: A shared molecular formula does not force a shared name; arrangement changes the name.

options.text: Isomers are named by adding numbers chosen at random
options.explanation: Position numbers follow fixed rules about where the group sits, never randomness.

options.text: Isomers cannot be named, so they are labelled A and B
options.explanation: The naming system handles isomers precisely; letter labels are not part of it.

questions.stem: What do the numbers in a branched name such as 2-methylbutane tell you?

options.text: Where the side chain sits relative to the main chain
options.explanation: The number fixes the position of the side chain along the main chain.

options.text: How many side chains the molecule has
options.explanation: Counting side chains is a separate job; the number locates a side chain.

options.text: The temperature at which the compound boils
options.explanation: Physical data is never encoded in the name.

options.text: The year the compound was first made
options.explanation: History plays no role in IUPAC names.

questions.stem: What level of naming is expected of you in this specification?

options.text: Name simple straight-chain compounds and unbranched isomers with up to six carbons
options.explanation: The expectation covers straightforward chains and unbranched isomers within six carbons.

options.text: Generate any branched name from scratch, however complex
options.explanation: Branched names may appear in questions, but you are not usually asked to build them yourself.

options.text: Name only the first two members of each family
options.explanation: The ceiling is six carbons, not two; meth and eth are just the first stems.

options.text: Write trade names instead of systematic names
options.explanation: The specification expects IUPAC systematic names, not trade labels.

questions.stem: State the prefix used when a molecule carries two of the same functional group.
questions.modelAnswer: The prefix di- is attached to the second part of the name for two identical groups.

questions.stem: What job do the numbers in an organic name do?
questions.modelAnswer: They give the position of the functional group or side chain along the carbon chain.

questions.stem: Explain how the naming rules separate two isomers that share one molecular formula.
questions.modelAnswer: The same rules are applied to each different structure in turn, so every isomer receives a name that reflects its own arrangement of atoms.

questions.stem: A name reads 2-chlorobutane. State how many carbons the chain has and what sits on carbon number 2.
questions.modelAnswer: But counts four carbons, and the 2 says a chlorine atom (the chloro group) sits on carbon number 2.
